title: Effects of Laser Welding on the Microstructure and Fatigue Behavior of Strenx 700 CR Steel
abstract: Abstract This study examines the cold-rolled microalloyed steel Strenx 700, with a minimum yield strength of 700 MPa, used in the manufacture of agricultural machinery and implements. The aim is to improve the weight/mechanical strength ratio and apply new advanced welding processes, such as laser welding. In the context of the agricultural machinery industry, laser welding is gaining prominence in the welding of thin microalloyed steels, mainly due to its small heat-affected zone and welding speed, which allow for superior mechanical properties, longer fatigue life, and excellent surface finish of welded joints compared to GMAW and GTAW welding processes. In this context, the behavior of laser-welded joints in Strenx 700 microalloyed steel was evaluated in the welding of plates used in agricultural implement components subjected to cyclic loads. The microstructural properties, mechanical properties, and fatigue life are not yet clearly documented in the literature. This work aimed to evaluate the performance of manual welds produced using a CO₂ laser process and to elucidate their effects on the microstructure, mechanical properties, and fatigue behavior of 2 mm thick Strenx 700 cold-rolled steel sheets. Based on technical evaluations through pre-tests, it was determined that the welds would be performed autogenously with welding powers of 1100, 1300, and 1500 Watts, using joints with parallel edge preparation without root opening, in order to optimize the processes and reduce industrial costs. After welding, joint characterization was performed using macrographs and micrographs obtained by optical and electron microscopy, in addition to microhardness mapping, tensile testing, and evaluation of uniaxial fatigue life in tension-tension conditions. The results indicate satisfactory macroscopic weld formation. In the fusion zone, the microstructure consisted predominantly of martensite, Widmanstätten ferrite and bainite. In the coarse-grained heat-affected zone (CGA), bainite, Widmanstätten ferrite, and martensite were observed, while in the fine-grained heat-affected zone (FGA), ferrite and martensite were identified. The base metal was composed of ferrite, bainite, and martensite. The mechanical strength of the welded joints was comparable to that of the base metal; however, the elongation values were lower than those of the base metal. The mean fatigue life of the base material was 450,128 cycles, significantly higher than that of the welded conditions, with average values of 50,055 cycles for the welded group (c), followed by group (b) with 44,962 cycles, while the welded group (a) presented a mean fatigue life of 30,338 cycles. As main conclusions, we can observe the good microstructural formation of the joints for all welding conditions, with adequate mechanical strength values, but with reduced elongation and predominant fracture in the heat-affected zone and in the fusion region. It is also possible to conclude that the average fatigue life values were lower for the welded conditions compared to the base material, this result being strongly impacted by the presence of welding defects related to the process.
journal: Lasers in Manufacturing and Materials Processing

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: High-strenght-low-alloy (HSLA) steels play an essential role in reducing the mass of metallic structures and are widely used in the manufacturing of truck bodies, railway freight cars, automotive chassis, ships, aircrafts and offshore structures. This is primarily because this class of steels enables the design of lighter structures throughout the reduction of the cross-sectional area of structural members, given their high mechanical strength and good toughness [ 1 ,  2 ,  3 ,  4 ].

These mechanical properties stem from a fine-grained microstructure achieved through thermomechanically controlled processing (TMCP), along with the presence of Ti, V and Nb based precipitates at grain boundaries. Among the numerous HSLA grades, Strenx 700 stands out due to its extensive use in the agricultural sector, exhibiting minimum values of 700 MPa for yield strength and 12% for elongation [ 1 ,  5 ,  6 ].

In addition to their mechanical properties, HSLA steels generally exhibit excellent weldability due to their low carbon content and reduced alloying levels. According to Prochenka et al. [ 7 ], the carbon equivalent of Strenx 700 is approximately 0.25%. At the same time, the possibility of using smaller cross sections in components reduces the number of joints and helps decrease filler metal consumption and operating time [ 8 ]. Nevertheless, welding of this class of alloys still presents challenges regarding the preservation of TMCP derived mechanical properties [ 7 ,  8 ,  9 ]. Accordingly, Bukovská et al. [ 1 ] recommend limiting the heat input to 10 kJ/cm in order to prevent embrittlement of the heat-affected zone (HAZ).

The thermal input associated with welding promotes grain growth in the heat-affected regions, which in itself tends to embrittle this zone, since one of the key factors responsible for the high mechanical strength of Strenx steels is their fine-grained microstructure [ 10 ,  11 ]. To mitigate this effect, multiple welding types with low heat input can be employed to reduce the likelihood of grain coarsening [ 12 ]. Another approach to alleviate this issue is the use of laser welding processes [ 3 ,  9 ].

In laser welding, the heat input is lower and more concentrated than in electric arc processes. According to Gunther et al. [ 14 ], a hand-held laser beam welding (HLBW) process operating at 1500 W and 45 cm/min exhibits a heat input on the order of 0.56 kJ/cm, which is lower than those typically obtained in other welding processes and also below the threshold proposed by Bukovská et al. [ 1 ]. This localized heat deposition markedly reduces distortion and the size of the heat-affected zone (HAZ), leading to smaller microstructural changes and, in many cases, less degradation of mechanical properties in this region.

In addition to improved thermal control, high welding precision, high productivity, high power density, and ease of integration with automated systems are factors that contribute to its prominence in manufacturing applications, particularly those involving thin sheets, since they directly affect the efficiency of production processes [ 14 ,  15 ,  16 ].

Furthermore, the mechanisms and operating conditions of laser welding differ substantially from those observed in conventional arc welding processes. Variations in equipment parameters, such as wavelength and power intensity, lead to different processing configurations, which must be adjusted according to the type of laser employed. These parameters directly influence the heating intensity, the surface melting mechanism, cooling and solidification rates, penetration depth, fusion zone morphology, the width-to-depth ratio, and the volume of molten metal [ 17 ,  18 ].

As stated by Szusta et al. [ 19 ], autogenous laser welding, performed without filler metal, when applied to joints of Strenx 700 and Strenx 1100 steels, is strongly influenced by the selected operating parameters. Although no cracking was observed, a reduction in microhardness in the heat-affected zone (HAZ) was verified, which directly affects the tensile strength and ductility of the material.

Recent studies have investigated the microstructural response and mechanical properties of HSLA steels welded using laser processes. In this context, Khanigi et al. [ 8 ] analyzed oscillating Nd: YAG laser welding under autogenous conditions applied to 2 mm thick Strenx 700 sheets. The authors reported the formation of distinct ferrite morphologies, as well as the presence of bainite and martensite. Regarding mechanical performance, the welded specimens exhibited an average ultimate tensile strength of 774 ± 14 MPa and an elongation of 26.5 ± 2.5%. Similarly, Gunther et al. [ 13 ] investigated the effects of fiber laser welding on 3 mm thick Strenx 700 sheets. The authors identified reductions in the mechanical properties of the specimens: yield strength decreased from 778 MPa in the as-received condition to 686 MPa in the welded specimens, while hardness also decreased from 280 HV to 240 HV.

Hardness values in the fusion region of laser welds can be dramatically increased by the large local heat input and the high cooling rate [ 20 ,  21 ]. In this context, the application of post-weld heat treatment to reduce hardness may be necessary in materials where there is an increase in hardness values in different areas of the weld [ 22 ,  23 ].

Regarding the fatigue life of Strenx 700, Šebestová et al. [ 24 ] reported that microstructural changes and the presence of surface notches generated by the laser welding process reduced both the applied load capacity and the number of cycles to failure of the specimens. In addition, they observed that crack initiation occurred preferentially at the interface between the fusion zone and the heat-affected zone (HAZ). Nevertheless, it is important to note that, as stated by Moe et al. [ 25 ], the use of laser welding, when compared with the GMAW process, can provide improved fatigue life for Strenx 700, Strenx 960, and Strenx 1100.

In this context, the present study sought to investigate the effects of autogenous CO 2  laser welding power on the welding of Strenx 700 CR steel applied in the manufacture of agricultural implement components subjected to mechanical fatigue stresses. To this end, three autogenous laser welding conditions were evaluated with powers of 1100, 1300, and 1500 Watts, aiming to assess their impact on the microstructural characteristics of the heat-affected zone regions, measurement of microhardness profiles in different weld areas, and mechanical tensile and fatigue tests to evaluate the static and dynamic behavior of the joints. This evaluation sought to identify the behavior of these joints for welding without filler metal and their impacts on quality and defect formation in manual laser welding. The application demands significant fatigue stresses, and the microstructures of the different regions of the joints, as well as the post-fracture aspects of the welded samples and the identification of welding defects, were evaluated using scanning electron microscopy. Therefore, this work aims to evaluate the feasibility of replacing GMAW welding with autogenous laser welding for the manufacture of agricultural implement components subject to fatigue loads.

sections.heading: Laser Welding Materials and Processes
paragraphs: The experimental investigation was based on CO₂ laser welding applied to Strenx 700 CR steel under different welding power levels. Microstructural and mechanical properties were examined, as well as the influence of process parameters on the integrity and performance of the welded joint.

The welding procedure was carried out on sheets measuring 300 mm in length, 150 mm in width, and 2 mm in thickness. Joint preparation was performed by machining, without a bevel, and welding was conducted with no root opening. The equipment used was an IPG Photonics LightWeld 1500 CO₂ laser welding machine, and the configuration obtained for the joints with powers of 1100, 1300, and 1500 Watts is shown in Fig.  1 .
Fig. 1 Laser welding equipment and configuration of welded joints

Welding was performed manually, with the operator using a guide to control the movement of the power source and a beam diameter of 2.5 mm. The welding direction was oriented towards the operator, using the tensile welding technique. The fixed and variable parameters adopted in this study are listed in Table  1 .

Table 1 Laser welding parameters Welding condition Laser power (W) Defocusing amount (mm) Average welding speed (m/min) Frequency (Hz) Shielding gas Shielding gas flow rate (l/min) Weld A 1100 0 0.72 4 99,99% Nitrogen 19 Weld B 1300 0 0.72 4 99,99% Nitrogen 19 Weld C 1500 0 0.72 4 99,99% Nitrogen 19
After welding, the specimens were extracted using laser cutting, leaving an allowance for subsequent finishing and removal of the heat-affected surface layer, as shown in Fig.  2 .
Fig. 2 Representation models test specimens

sections.heading: Microstructural and Mechanical Properties
paragraphs: After specimen preparation, the material’s chemical composition was first determined using an Oxford Foundry-Master X-Line optical emission spectrometer. The chemical composition is presented in Table  2 , detailing the constituent elements.
Table 2 Nominal chemical composition of Strenx 700 CR microalloyed steel Alloys Elements (wt%) Fe C Si Mn P S Al Nb Ti Measured Strenx 700 CR Bal. 0.15 0.14 1.5 0.010 0.010 0.17 0.009 0.005

The next stage comprised metallographic analysis. From the extracted specimens, mounts were prepared in Bakelite resin and sequentially ground using #150, 220, 400, 600, 1000, and 2000 grit SiC papers. Polishing was performed on a polishing machine using a 1 μm alumina suspension. Metallographic etching was carried out with 10% nital for 10 s for macrographic examinations, 2% nital for 15 s for optical micrographs, and 2% nital for 20 s for SEM microstructural analysis. Macrographs were obtained using an Olympus SZ61 stereomicroscope, and optical micrographs were acquired using an Olympus BX51M optical microscope. The sheet microstructure was examined using a Tescan Vega LM3 scanning electron microscope (SEM), shown in Fig.  3 , revealing a microstructure consisting of ferrite, bainite with aggregated carbides and martensite.
Fig. 3 Microstructure of base metal Strenx 700 CR microalloyed steel plate

After the microscopy analyses, the same specimens were subjected to microhardness testing in accordance with ASTM E384. Measurements were performed on the transverse cross-section at the center of the joint using the Vickers microhardness method. A load of 0.3 kgf was applied with a dwell time of 15 s, and an indentation spacing of 0.2 mm was used to scan the different weld regions.

To evaluate the mechanical strength of the welded joints and the base metal, tensile tests were performed in accordance with ASTM E8M using standardized specimens as shown in Fig.  4 . The tests were conducted on a Shenk UPM 200 universal testing machine. Three specimens were tested for the base metal and three specimens for each welding condition. All specimens were tested under uniaxial loading at a crosshead speed of 0.5 mm/min.
Fig. 4 Tensile test specimen model

The fatigue tests were conducted in accordance with ASTM E466, using specimens with the geometry shown in Fig.  5 . The tests were performed on a Shimadzu servo-hydraulic testing machine, model EHF-EV101. The maximum load applied in the tensile cycle was defined as 50% of the maximum stress for each tested group, adopting a fatigue ratio of 0.1 and a testing frequency of 3 Hz.
Fig. 5 Fatigue test specimen model

After the fatigue tests, the fractured specimens were analyzed by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) in order to evaluate the fracture surfaces. The samples were carefully removed and kept intact during preparation, so as to preserve their original surface characteristics.

sections.heading: Macroscopic Analysis of Welded Joints
paragraphs: The macroscopic profiles of the welded joints are presented in Fig.  6  and subdivided into three conditions according to the energy input: weld A (1100 W), weld B (1300 W), and weld C (1500 W). The depth-to-width ratio indicates the occurrence of full penetration in all welds.In all three conditions, a surface depression was observed on the upper side of the weld bead, which may be associated with excessive energy input or overpenetration, as well as possible imprecision in controlling the welding speed along the weld seam due to the application of a manual process.

Although higher heat input is generally associated with the formation of a wider heat-affected zone (HAZ) with coarser microstructures, as reported by Qi et al. [ 26 ], equivalent HAZ dimensions were observed among the three welding conditions. This behavior can be attributed to the lack of strict control over the welding speed, which is characteristic of the manual process employed. The HAZ cross-sectional length was 0.723 ± 0.128 mm for weld A, 0.813 ± 0.055 mm for weld B, and 0.774 ± 0.079 mm for weld C.
Fig. 6 Upper surface and profiles of joints welded with different powers: ( a ) 1100 W, ( b ) 1300 W and ( c ) 1500 W

sections.heading: Microstructural Analysis of Welded Joints
paragraphs: The microstructural analysis was performed based on images obtained by optical microscopy and scanning electron microscopy (SEM), which allowed the identification and differentiation of the welding zones. The regions were subdivided into the fusion zone (FZ), coarse-microstructure heat-affected zone (HAZCG), fine-grained heat-affected zone (HAZFG), and base material (BM), as illustrated in Figs.  7  and  8 , and  9 .

For weld A, with a power of 1100 W, shown in Fig.  7 , the FZ exhibits the formation of martensite (M), bainite (B) and Widmanstätten ferrite (WF), characterizing a coarse microstructure resulting from material melting. The HAZCG region presented a microstructure composed of lath martensite, granular bainite, and Widmanstätten ferrite, indicating complete austenitization of this region. In the HAZFG region, the microstructure is predominantly composed of ferrite, with a minor presence of martensite, which promotes a reduction in the local hardness of the material due to the mechanical properties of ferrite. Finally, the microstructure of the base material (BM) consisted of ferrite, bainite, and martensite, in agreement with the initial condition of the material.
Fig. 7 Microstructure of the joint welded ( a ) with the power of 1100 W

For weld B, with a power of 1300 W, whose microstructures are shown in Fig.  8 , the fusion zone (FZ) exhibits a predominant presence of martensite (M), Widmanstätten ferrite (WF) and bainite (B). In the coarse- microstructure heat-affected zone (HAZCG), in addition to Widmanstätten ferrite and bainite, the presence of martensite (M) is also identified. The fine-grained heat-affected zone (HAZFG) presents martensite (M) dispersed within a ferritic matrix. In turn, the base material (BM) exhibits a mixed microstructure composed of ferrite, bainite, and martensite. In their study, Pandey et al. [ 24 ] observed the formation of different compounds in the fusion zone of welded steels, indicating the formation of fine precipitates, ferrite, martensite, and bainite, suggesting various modifications in the fusion region of the welded materials.
Fig. 8 Microstructure of the joint welded ( b ) with the power of 1300 W

Fig. 9 Microstructure of the joint welded ( c ) with the power of 1500 W Finally. the microstructures of weld C, produced with a power of 1500 W, are presented in Fig. 9. In the fusion zone, (FZ), the presence of martensite, (M), Widmanstätten ferrite, (WF) and bainite, (B) is identified. In the coarse-grained and fine-grained heat-affected zones, (HAZCG and HAZFG), a concomitant presence of ferrite and fine martensite is observed, with ferrite being predominant in the HAZFG and martensite predominant in the HAZCG. Studies conducted by Lian Chen et al. [ 27 ] reported the formation of martensite, acicular ferrite and bainite under higher heat inputs, whereas, for lower heat input conditions, a predominantly martensitic microstructure was observed in the fusion zone of laser-welded materials

sections.heading: Mechanical Properties of Welded Joints
paragraphs: The microhardness profiles along the transverse cross-section of the welded joints are presented in Fig.  10 . For the weld produced at a power of 1100 W, Fig.  10  (a), the heat-affected zone (HAZ) exhibited an average microhardness value of 221 HV, which is significantly lower than that of the base material (274 HV). In contrast, the fusion zone showed an average value of 375 HV. This pronounced reduction in microhardness in the HAZ indicates local softening associated with microstructural transformations induced by the welding thermal cycle. Under the 1300 W condition, Fig.  10  (b), the HAZ presented an average microhardness value of 226 HV, again lower than those of the base material (261 HV) and the fusion zone (357 HV), confirming the occurrence of HAZ softening for this welding condition as well. For the weld produced at a power of 1500 W, Fig.  10  (c), the average microhardness value in the HAZ was 255 HV, close to that of the base material (266 HV), while the fusion zone exhibited the highest average value among the evaluated conditions (396 HV). This result evidences a less severe reduction in HAZ microhardness when compared to welds produced at lower power levels. Overall, increasing the welding energy contributed to mitigating HAZ softening, with the 1500 W condition showing the smallest decrease in microhardness values in this region. The fusion zone microhardness values remained high under all conditions, with a slight reduction observed for the weld produced at a power of 1300 W.
Fig. 10 Hardness profiles of joints welded at ( a ) 1100 W, ( b ) 1300 W and ( c ) 1500 W

The hardness profile along the welded joint is directly associated with the microstructural transformations induced by the thermal cycle. In the fusion zone (FZ), the high hardness is mainly attributed to the formation of a course microstructure of Widmanstätten ferrite, martensite and bainite, reaching values close to 400 HV in laser welding of S700MC steel, significantly exceeding that of the base metal [ 8 ]. In contrast, in the heat-affected zone (HAZ), particularly in the fine-grained region, the lowest hardness values are observed (below 240 HV), associated with a predominantly ferritic matrix containing islands of granular Martensite–Austenite (M–A) constituent [ 13 ]. This softening is related to the decomposition of original martensitic and bainitic constituents into polygonal ferrite and fractions of M–A, with the increase in ferrite fraction being the main factor responsible for the reduction in local mechanical strength [ 13 ]. Nevertheless, the presence of TiN particles and Nb/Ti carbonitrides acts to control grain growth through a pinning effect, partially mitigating the loss of hardness in these regions [ 8 ].

The results of the tensile tests are presented in Table  3 . Welding condition (A) exhibited high mechanical strength, with an average ultimate tensile strength of 1030 MPa, a value close to that of the base material (1077 MPa). However, a significant reduction in elongation was observed, decreasing from 9.96% in the base material to 2.75% in the welded joint. Fractures occurred predominantly in the heat-affected zone (HAZ), as indicated in Fig.  11  (a), suggesting that microstructural modifications associated with the local reduction in microhardness favored fracture nucleation and propagation in this region. Welding under condition (B) resulted in an average ultimate tensile strength of 915 MPa, accompanied by a high standard deviation, and an average elongation of 2.46%. In all specimens, fracture occurred in the fusion zone, as shown in Fig.  11  (b). This behavior indicates a low capacity for plastic deformation, associated with microstructural embrittlement of the fusion zone, possibly aggravated by the presence of fusion defects. For welding condition (C), an average ultimate tensile strength of 994 MPa and an average elongation of 2.57% were observed, with fracture located in the HAZ, as presented in Fig.  11  (c). This result suggests that the reduction in microhardness in this region, resulting from microstructural transformations induced by the welding thermal cycle, contributed to stress concentration and subsequent fracture.

Fig. 11 Cross-sections of the samples after the tensile tests

Figure  12 , obtained by stereomicroscopy, macroscopically evidences the presence of welding defects along the transverse cross-section of the welded joint. Discontinuities in the weld metal, indicated by arrows, are observed and are predominantly associated with lack of fusion and internal discontinuities, non-uniformly distributed along the weld bead.

Instabilities during the laser welding process, especially under poorly controlled operating conditions, are directly associated with the formation of defects that compromise the mechanical integrity of the joints. In the analyzed case, these instabilities can be attributed to the combination of applied power, variations in welding speed, and, primarily, the manual nature of the process. The lack of strict control over the travel speed promotes an uneven energy distribution along the weld bead, hindering complete fusion at the interfaces and favoring the formation of discontinuities [ 13 ].

The laser power density stands out as the most influential parameter affecting both process stability and the mechanical strength of the joint [ 14 ]. An excessive increase in average power may induce intense metal vaporization, combined with the high cooling rates typical of laser welding, this hinders the escape of vapor from the molten pool, resulting in pore formation after solidification [ 8 ].

To mitigate these effects, the use of a defocused beam without lateral oscillation is recommended, along with nitrogen as a shielding gas, since it exhibits higher solubility in the molten pool compared to argon, thereby promoting the reduction of internal porosity. Furthermore, instabilities in beam control also manifest as surface geometric discontinuities, such as undercuts, misalignments, and irregular weld bead reinforcement [ 13 ].

From a mechanical standpoint, both internal and surface defects act as stress concentrators, reducing the effective load-bearing cross-section of the joint. Under cyclic loading, these discontinuities become preferential sites for fatigue crack initiation [ 13 ,  24 ]. To mitigate lack of fusion, as observed in Fig.  12 , the heat input must be optimized to operate in keyhole mode, ensuring full penetration [ 7 ,  17 ]. In pulsed lasers, increasing the overlap factor raises the effective energy density, facilitating deeper remelting of the joint [ 7 ]. Hybrid Laser-TIG welding assists in gap bridging [Sebestova]. It is essential to avoid excessively low linear energy inputs, which leave the root at the penetration threshold, ensuring complete fusion through the material thickness [ 17 ].
Fig. 12 Stereoscopic image of defects

The reduction in tensile strength of welded joints, particularly in thermomechanically processed high-strength steels, results from a combination of microstructural transformations and geometric alterations induced by the welding thermal cycle. The heat input during welding promotes a softening phenomenon in the heat-affected zone (HAZ), where hardness and strength decrease significantly compared to the base metal [ 2 ,  28 ]. This loss in strength can reach up to 15% of the original tensile strength of the material [ 2 ]. In S700 steel, the fine-grained subzone is often the weakest region, exhibiting a microstructure composed of polygonal ferrite and islands of granular Martensite–Austenite (M–A) constituent, which possess a lower load-bearing capacity than the microstructure of the base material [ 13 ]. In tensile tests, failure commonly occurs in these regions of lower local microhardness within the HAZ [ 17 ]. In parallel, weld geometry, such as excessive reinforcement, undercut, or misalignment, creates structural notches that act as stress concentrators. Although these defects severely affect ductility and fatigue life, they can also facilitate crack initiation, thereby reducing the static load-bearing capacity of the joint [ 24 ].

sections.heading: Fatigue Tests of Base Material and Welded Joints
paragraphs: The results of the fatigue tests for the base material and for welding conditions (A), (B), and (C) are presented in Table  4 . The base material exhibited the highest average number of cycles to failure (456,128 cycles), whereas the welded joints showed significantly inferior performance, with average values of 30,338 cycles for condition (A), 44,962 cycles for condition (B), and 50,050 cycles for condition (C).

The tests were conducted under maximum stress levels corresponding to 50% of the ultimate tensile strength of each group, adopting a fatigue ratio of 0.1. The applied stresses were individually adjusted for each condition, as indicated in Table  4 . For all welding conditions, fatigue fracture initiated in the weld metal, indicating the presence of embrittled regions associated with the welding process.

A high standard deviation in the number of cycles to failure was observed for all welded conditions, reflecting the variability inherent to the manual process and the presence of discontinuities. To better interpret the results, a statistical analysis using Tukey’s test was performed and is presented in Table  5 . The statistical results indicated superior performance of the base material, classified in group A, whereas the welded conditions were grouped in group B, with no statistically significant differences among them.

Table 5 Tukey test of fatigue results for base material, weld (A), weld (B) and weld (C) Fatigue group N Mean cicles Grouping Base material 5 456,128 A Weld C 5 50,055 B Weld B 5 44,962 B Weld A 5 30,338 B

For the analysis of the fracture surfaces of the base material and the welded joints, the specimens that exhibited the lowest number of cycles to failure under each condition were selected. For the base material, Fig.  13 , crack initiation was observed at the lateral edge of the specimen after 368,374 cycles, characterizing a typical fatigue behavior for a material free of welding defects. For welding condition (A), shown in Fig.  14 , the presence of a pronounced lack-of-fusion defect in the weld metal was identified, which acted as a preferential site for crack initiation. This defect limited the fatigue life of the joint to only 12,564 cycles, highlighting its critical role in premature failure. The fractographic analysis of welding condition (B), presented in Fig.  15 , revealed large lack-of-fusion regions formed during the welding process. Although these discontinuities were not distributed along the entire weld bead, they acted as severe stress concentrators, resulting in premature fracture after 6,273 cycles. Similarly, welding condition (C), shown in Fig.  16 , also exhibited fatigue failure initiation associated with a lack-of-fusion defect, with the fatigue life limited to 7,690 cycles, again characterizing premature fracture behavior.

Fig. 14 Fracture surface after fatigue test samples from welding condition A
Fig. 15 Fracture surface after fatigue test samples from welding condition B
Fig. 16 Fracture surface after fatigue test samples from welding condition C

sections.heading: Discussion
paragraphs: The main objective of the present work was to evaluate the microstructures of laser-welded joints and the fatigue behavior of these joints in comparison with the base material. Microstructural analyses evidenced the formation of three distinct regions in the welded joints, the fusion zone (FZ), coarse-microstructure heat-affected zone (HAZCG), and fine- microstructure heat-affected zone (HAZFG), in addition to the base material, as shown in Figs.  7  and  8 , and  9  for welding conditions (A), (B) and (C).

For all evaluated conditions, the FZ exhibited microstructures characterized by the presence of martensite, Widmanstätten ferrite and bainite, associated with the melting and solidification thermal cycle. In the HAZCG, martensite, bainite, and Widmanstätten ferrite were observed, indicating complete austenitization and pronounced grain growth due to temperatures exceeding the Ac₃ line. In contrast, the HAZFG presented a microstructure predominantly composed of ferrite and martensite, resulting from temperatures close to Ac₃, promoting smaller variations in grain size and a gradual transition to the base material under all welding conditions.

Analysis of microhardness profiles revealed a significant reduction in hardness values in the HAZFG (fine- microstructure heat-affected zone) for the lower welding power conditions, (A) and (B), as shown in Fig.  10 . Under these conditions, the average microhardness values in the HAZ were substantially lower than those of the base material, while the FZ (fused zone) showed a marked increase in hardness mainly due to the formation of larger amounts of martensite, Widmanstätten ferrite and bainite with the formation of a coarse microstructure in this region. For welding condition (C), with higher power, a less pronounced reduction in HAZ microhardness was observed, resulting in values closer to those of the base material. This behavior was attributed to the greater local heating that provided higher cooling rates, generating a microstructure with greater hardness.

Tensile tests indicated similar mechanical strength values for the base material and the welded joints. However, elongation was significantly higher for the base material, indicating greater ductility compared to the welded conditions. Fracture occurred predominantly in the HAZ for conditions (A) and (C), whereas for condition (B) fracture took place in the weld metal, indicating a stronger influence of welding defects in this region.

Regarding fatigue performance, the base material exhibited markedly superior behavior, with a higher average number of cycles to failure. In contrast, the welded joints presented inferior and statistically comparable fatigue performance, along with a pronounced scatter in the results. Fractographic analysis indicated that fatigue crack initiation occurred predominantly in regions containing welding defects, such as lack of fusion, as illustrated in Figs.  13 ,  14 ,  15  and  16 . These defects, qualitatively identified at the crack nucleation sites, act as stress concentrators, facilitating both crack initiation and propagation, and thus represent the primary factor responsible for the reduced fatigue life of the welded joints compared to the base material.

Further analysis of the fracture surfaces revealed that crack nucleation preferentially occurs at the interfaces between the base metal and the HAZ. According to Sebestova et al. [ 23 ], this behavior is closely related to the weld bead geometry, as discontinuities such as excessive reinforcement, undercut, and misalignment act as severe stress concentrators. Additionally, the inherently irregular surface topography of Strenx 700 steel contributes to both crack initiation and its accelerated propagation.

Even in ground specimens, failure in laser-welded Strenx 700 joints tends to localize at the interface between the fusion zone (FZ) and the HAZ. This behavior is attributed to the presence of microconstituents such as martensite and bainite, combined with a relatively lower degree of grain refinement, which promotes strain localization under cyclic loading induced by the welding thermal cycles [ 23 ]. Furthermore, studies on laser-welded Strenx 700 indicate that the combined effects of residual stresses and microstructural modifications are the main factors responsible for the reduction in fatigue life [ 1 ].

In this context, the development of more homogeneous microstructures is beneficial for improving the fatigue performance of welded joints. Conversely, the presence of softened zones favors the formation of cleavage facets, thereby facilitating crack nucleation and ultimately reducing the material’s resistance to cyclic loading [ 27 ,  28 ].

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: This study evaluated the influence of welding power on the microstructure and fatigue behavior of autogenous laser-welded joints, without root opening, in Strenx 700 CR steel. The main conclusions can be summarized as follows:

Macrographic analysis indicated an increase in surface concavity of the weld beads with increasing welding power, being more pronounced for the 1300 W and 1500 W conditions. The microstructures observed qualitatively under the different welding conditions do not show significant differences and were characterized by the presence of martensite, Widmanstätten ferrite and bainite in the fusion zone (FZ), bainite, ferrite, and martensite in the coarse-microstructure heat-affected zone (HAZCG), and ferrite and martensite in the fine-grained heat-affected zone (HAZFG). A reduction in microhardness was observed in the HAZ for all welding conditions, being more pronounced for the lowest welding power condition, corresponding to weld (A). Tensile tests indicated fracture in the HAZ for welds (A) and (C), whereas for weld (B) fracture occurred in the fusion zone, a behavior attributed to the higher incidence of welding defects under this condition. Ultimate tensile strength values were similar between the base material (1077 MPa) and the welded joints (1030 MPa, 915 MPa, and 994 MPa for conditions (A), (B), and (C), respectively). However, all welded conditions exhibited a significant reduction in elongation compared to the base material (9.96%), with values ranging from 2.46% to 2.75%. Under controlled tension–tension cyclic loading, the base material exhibited statistically superior fatigue performance, with an average of 456,128 cycles to failure and classification in group A. The welded conditions showed inferior fatigue performance, with average values of 50,055 cycles for weld (C), 44,962 cycles for weld (B), and 30,338 cycles for weld (A). Welding defects associated with lack of fusion were identified as the main factor responsible for fatigue crack initiation, significantly contributing to the high dispersion of results and to the inferior fatigue performance of the welded joints compared to the base material.
